displayQuote: Substitute 'Damn' Every Time You're Inclined to Write 'Very'

meta.title: Who really said "Substitute 'Damn' Every Time You're Inclined to Write 'Very'"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Mark Twain, and not Franklin P. Adams. Newspapers from the 1920s–40s credit the joke to editor William Allen White. In a 1946 version, Adams is only the listener.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Substitute 'Damn' Every Time You're Inclined to Write 'Very''?
meta.ogDescription: Not Mark Twain or Franklin P. Adams. Quote Investigator traces the 'damn'-for-'very' advice to Kansas editor William Allen White, with indirect evidence.

answer.label: Not Mark Twain — credited to William Allen White
answer.sourceLine: Quote Investigator’s best candidate is the Emporia editor William Allen White. A 1935 Seattle Daily Times column tells of him giving the advice to cub reporters. A 1946 retelling has White giving it to Franklin P. Adams, so Adams is the listener, not the author. QI calls the evidence indirect, and the popular “your editor will delete it” wording is a later paraphrase.

source.heading: The earliest full telling

docMeta.dd: Seattle Daily Times, “Strolling Around the Town,” 18 October 1935
Orrville Courier Crescent (Ohio), 19 December 1946. White tells the joke to Franklin P. Adams

source.excerpt: “I never give advice,” said Mr. White, “but there is one thing I wish you would do when you sit down to write news stories, and that is: Never use the word, ‘very.’ It is the weakest word in the English language; doesn’t mean anything. If you feel the urge of ‘very’ coming on, just write the word, ‘damn,’ in the place of ‘very.’ The editor will strike out the word, ‘damn,’ and you will have a good sentence.”
trail: 1922: The Pittsburgh Press prints a quip: “Will Allen White advises the use of ‘damn’ in place of ‘very.’” (Quote Investigator ↗)

1935: a Seattle Daily Times column gives the full anecdote. White advises cub reporters in Lawrence, Kansas, to write “damn” in place of “very,” because the editor will strike it out (Quote Investigator ↗)

1946–47: a retelling has White giving the advice to Franklin P. Adams. Reader’s Digest prints a version in January 1947, credited to “Brock Pemberton, quoted in Kansas City Star” (Quote Investigator ↗)
Today: quote sites carry a smoothed version (“your editor will delete it and the writing will be just as it should be”) and often credit Mark Twain, as Goodreads does ↗
source.excerptNote: As transcribed by Quote Investigator from the Seattle Daily Times, 18 October 1935. The columnist says the meeting with young newspapermen in Lawrence, Kansas, happened “several years ago.”

sourceLink.text: Quote Investigator: the full chronology of the ‘damn’ for ‘very’ advice

source.rightsNote: The popular wording is a paraphrase of unknown origin; it does not appear in any period text Quote Investigator transcribes, so no rights status can be claimed for it. The 1935 and 1946 newspaper versions are worded differently, and both are retellings by unnamed columnists, not White’s own writing.

author.name: William Allen White
author.heading: About William Allen White
author.metaLine: 1868–1944 · Editor of the Emporia Gazette, Kansas
author.bio: William Allen White bought the Emporia Gazette and edited it for the rest of his life. That made him “the Sage of Emporia” and a national voice for middle America and the Progressive movement. He won a Pulitzer Prize for his 1922 editorial “To an Anxious Friend.” Newspapers from 1922 on credit him with the advice to swap “damn” for “very.”

misattribution.heading: Why Twain (and Adams) get named
misattribution.intro: This writing tip has passed through several famous names. None of them is backed by a source in that person’s own words.

items.why: In the 1946 Orrville Courier Crescent version, White “once told Franklin P. Adams” how to get rid of the word. That makes Adams the person receiving the advice. In every version Quote Investigator ↗ cites, Adams is the listener; none has him saying or writing it. Adams’s Wikiquote page ↗ does not list it.

Quote Investigator ↗ found no substantive evidence that Twain said it, and notes the line is not on the Twain Quotes website edited by Barbara Schmidt. Even so, sites such as Goodreads ↗ credit Twain.

Reader’s Digest (January 1947) printed the Adams version under the credit “Brock Pemberton, quoted in Kansas City Star.” Quote Investigator ↗ suggests this may be where that version came from. The joke itself is still White’s.

misattribution.truthLine: The advice is credited to William Allen White from 1922 on, and the 1935 Seattle Daily Times has the full anecdote. Quote Investigator ↗ calls White the best candidate but says the evidence is not direct.

context.heading: Why the joke works
lead: The joke is a piece of newsroom craft. “Very” adds nothing, so a writer who puts “damn” in its place hands the editor a word that will certainly be cut. What is left is the stronger sentence. The 1935 telling has White calling “very” “the weakest word in the English language.”

In the newspapers Quote Investigator found, the story always stays with White, while the listener changes: first unnamed cub reporters in Kansas, later Franklin P. Adams. QI suggests White may simply have told the joke more than once.
context.pull: The editor will strike out the word, ‘damn,’ and you will have a good sentence.
